narrative:
The model estimated a 75.2% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure to be substantially more likely than success, so your law school application was denied on that risk basis. This is a probability, not a certainty, and gender and race were not used in the decision.

The strongest driver was your third-year class standing. You were in the second decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile; this was the most influential factor and pushed the prediction toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important factor and pushed toward passing: at 3.20, it was essentially in line with the accepted-student average of 3.23, so it helped your case but was not enough to outweigh the academic-standing concern. Your first-year class standing was the third most influential factor and also pushed toward failure, again placing you in the second decile versus an accepted-student average around the sixth decile.

To strengthen a future application, ask admissions for feedback, consider retaking the LSAT—your 34 was below the accepted average of about 37—and provide context for any early academic difficulties. You might also strengthen your record through relevant work, graduate coursework, or a stronger test score before reapplying.
